ShanghaiTech University; ByteDance, China; Shanghai AI Laboratory (academia and industry)

Proposes an evaluation method; secondary: Compares — SessionFarmer, an automated framework that turns in-the-wild developer-agent (vibe coding) sessions and repository checkpoints into executable SWE benchmark tasks (episode reconstruction, environment, task statement, rubrics, refined tests); builds CropChat (242 public tasks) and CropEnterprise (56 internal tasks); validates artefacts (requirement coverage, test accuracy, developer audit) and evaluates 12 model-harness configurations

No SDD approach. Evaluated configurations: 4 models (gpt-5.5-2026-04-24, gpt-5.6-terra, glm-5.2, kimi-k3) x 3 open-source harnesses (Codex 0.149.1, Pi 0.84.2, OpenCode 1.18.23), reasoning effort Medium; all 12 on CropChat, 3 gpt-5.6-terra configurations on CropEnterprise. Construction pipeline: Pi 0.84.2 with gpt-5.6-sol (high effort) for agent roles; deepseek-v4-flash-0731 for single-call judgments and the quality judge

N/A (no approach). Benchmark artefacts per task: base repository snapshot, self-contained task statement as a flat list of atomic requirement clauses ('obligations', each citing supporting conversation events), frozen offline Docker environment, hidden unit-test suite, hidden engineering-quality rubrics (Clarity, Design, Repository fit), requirement-breaking mutants, gold patch

N/A (no approach). SessionFarmer pipeline: (a) episode reconstruction (work clusters, LLM session relevance filtering, LLM episode partitioning, qualification); (b) environment reconstruction (Environment Builder, offline validation); (c) task statement and rubric authoring (Task Author, LLM validator, gold quality gate, mutants); (d) test construction (Test Author, criteria-based and blind-solver refinement). Evaluation: agent gets base repo and statement, single autonomous rollout within 2,700 s

None during agent runs or pipeline (fully automated). Post-hoc audit: 4 full-time engineers who authored the original code reviewed 28 CropEnterprise tasks (2 reviewers each, 56 reviews) for episode boundaries, sessions, statements and rubrics
Full autonomous agent runs on all tasks (3 rollouts per configuration); SessionFarmer run end to end; no SDD approach exercised
Not classifiable (no SDD approach; tasks are given as synthesized self-contained specifications of requirement clauses, but the authors do not use SDD terms)
Existing code base: tasks start from a base repository checkpoint of real repositories (CropEnterprise: 32 bug fixes, 22 feature implementations, 2 refactorings)

CropChat: 242 tasks, 61 repositories, 14 languages; mean 1.17 sessions, statement 374.2 words, gold patch 12.0 files / 904.2 lines (median 8 files / 411 lines), 11.67 unit tests (median 11); 100-5,000 implementation lines per episode. CropEnterprise: 56 tasks from 375 sessions in one TypeScript repository (1,592 source files, 473.3k LOC), median 9.5 files / 319.5 lines
Real-world open-source repositories from the public SWE-Chat dataset (mostly TypeScript and Go) and an internal enterprise development-platform monorepo (ByteDance)

For every configuration: quality verdict: no criterion stated by the authors; cost verdict: no criterion stated by the authors. Ablation (benchmark construction): test suites without refinement vs SessionFarmer on 30 CropChat tasks, BAcc 61.9 vs 70.8 (terra solver) and 53.3 vs 60.5 (gpt-5.5). Ablation (statement evidence): full requirement coverage on multi-session tasks 26% (first message), 54% (first session), 75% (full episode); single-session 49% vs 78%

Tasks: CropChat (242) and CropEnterprise (56). Configurations: 4 models x 3 harnesses (12) on CropChat; 3 terra configurations on CropEnterprise. Baseline: none for agents (test-refinement ablation compared with initial suites and with SWE-Bench-Pro and DeepSWE official suites). Held constant: task statements, frozen environments, 4 vCPU / 8 GB containers, 2,700 s limit, reasoning effort Medium, no temperature override, project-level OpenCode configs and Codex hooks disabled, repository instruction files kept. Acceptance tests: hidden synthesized and refined unit tests plus LLM quality gate. Repetitions: 3 independent rollouts per task and configuration. Human intervention: none

kimi-k3 + Codex best (Pass@1 39.3%); kimi-k3 leads under every harness and beats the other models by 9.6-12.4 pp harness-averaged; harness sensitivity model-dependent: gpt-5.5 and terra vary 1.1-1.2 pp, glm-5.2 3.2 pp, kimi-k3 drops 8.4 pp from Codex to Pi (timeouts 6.1% to 12.7%). terra fastest (median 4.2-4.8 min, 0.86-1.11M input tokens). Quality gate rejects 2.1% of test-passing rollouts on CropChat vs 12.6% on CropEnterprise (OpenCode QualityResolved 16.0 pp below Codex). 22.8% of task-configuration pairs inconsistent across 3 runs; 26.0% of tasks unsolved across all 36 rollouts; larger gold diffs and longer statements lower solve rates (rho about -0.42). No significance tests between configurations

Distinguished models clearly (kimi-k3 vs others) and showed harness effects for some models; between gpt-5.5, terra and glm-5.2 differences are small. Repeated (3 rollouts) and run-to-run variance reported (Pass3, within-task time SD 2.2-4.8 min). Authors conclude reliable comparisons need models and harnesses evaluated jointly and multi-run reporting; no other limitations of the comparison stated

No limitations or threats-to-validity section. Gaps / future uses: learning from real developer-agent experience (experience reuse, skills), comparing original interactive sessions with autonomous rollouts, underspecified task variants with user simulators, verifiable training environments for reinforcement learning; 63 CropChat tasks unsolved by any configuration as a failure-analysis set
